questions.text: Do you own a residential investment property (a rental, not the home you live in)?

options.label: Yes — bought (or signed the contract) before Budget night, 12 May 2026
Yes — an established property bought after 12 May 2026
Yes — a newly built property, or I'm planning to buy/build new

questions.text: Do you expect to sell assets — shares, property, a business — for a significant capital gain in the coming years?

options.label: Yes — mostly assets I already own today
Yes — mostly assets I'll buy from here on
Yes — startup equity or founder shares with a very low cost base

questions.text: Do you receive income distributions from a trust?

options.label: Yes — from a testamentary trust (set up by a will) that existed on 12 May 2026
Yes — from a special disability trust or a deceased estate

none.title: Negative gearing: doesn't apply to you
none.body: Like more than 8 in 10 Australian taxfilers, you own no investment property — so the negative gearing change can't touch you. In 2022–23, about 2.26 million individuals (out of roughly 16 million who lodged returns) had an interest in a rental property.

before.title: Negative gearing: you're grandfathered
before.body: Properties acquired (by contract date) before 7:30pm on 12 May 2026 are not affected. You can keep negatively gearing this property exactly as before — the change only applies to established properties bought after Budget night.

after-established.title: Negative gearing: this change applies to you
after-established.body: For established properties bought after Budget night, rental losses from 1 July 2027 are quarantined: they can only offset rental income or capital gains from rental property, not your salary. The losses aren't lost — they carry forward.

new-build.title: Negative gearing: new builds keep full negative gearing
new-build.body: The reform deliberately preserves — and channels — negative gearing toward new construction. A new build can still be negatively geared against your other income, and you can choose between the 50% CGT discount and the new arrangements.

none.title: Capital gains: little to no impact
none.body: If you're not expecting significant capital gains, this change barely touches you. Around 83% of the benefit of the current 50% CGT discount goes to the top 10% of taxpayers by income.

existing.title: Capital gains: your existing gains keep the 50% discount
existing.body: Gains accrued before 1 July 2027 retain the 50% discount even if you sell later — only growth after that date moves to indexation plus the 30% minimum rate. A valuation at 1 July 2027 (or an ATO formula) splits the two.

future.title: Capital gains: the new rules will apply to you
future.body: For assets bought from here on, you'll pay tax only on real (above-inflation) gains, at a minimum 30% rate. Whether that's better or worse than the 50% discount depends on how fast the asset grows relative to inflation — for modest, steady growth the difference is small; for very fast growth the new rules tax more of the gain.

startup.title: Capital gains: you're in the genuine edge case
startup.body: Indexation is harsh for fast-appreciating assets with a near-zero cost base — startup equity is the textbook example. This is a real design problem, and the Government has confirmed it is examining a targeted fix for small and startup businesses. See the honest caveats section below.

none.title: Trusts: doesn't apply to you
none.body: About 5% of individual taxfilers received discretionary trust distributions in 2022–23. By the Government's own estimate, more than 95% of taxfilers won't be affected by this change in any given year — and if you receive no trust income, that includes you.

discretionary.title: Trusts: this change applies to you
discretionary.body: From 1 July 2028, distributions from discretionary trusts are taxed at a minimum of 30%. If you're a beneficiary on a marginal rate below 30% (often the result of income splitting), the tax on those distributions rises to 30%. If your marginal rate is already 30% or above, little changes.

testamentary.title: Trusts: testamentary trusts existing at Budget night are excluded
testamentary.body: Testamentary trusts in existence on 12 May 2026 are carved out of the minimum tax — as are deceased estates and special disability trusts. Despite the 'death tax' framing, the measure does not tax inheritance at all.

excluded.title: Trusts: your trust is explicitly excluded
excluded.body: Special disability trusts and deceased estates are excluded from the minimum tax, along with charitable trusts, fixed and widely held trusts, and complying super funds.

benefits.heading: And the other side of the ledger
benefits.intro: These reforms aren't only about who loses a concession — the same Budget returns money to workers and redirects support toward housing supply. If you earn income from work, these apply to you:

items.title: A $1,000 instant deduction, no receipts
items.body: From 2026–27, anyone with work income can claim a flat $1,000 deduction for work-related expenses without keeping a single receipt. If your real expenses are higher, you can still itemise as before.

items.title: The Working Australians Tax Offset
items.body: From 2027–28, a permanent offset of up to $250 a year for income earned from work. Around 13 million workers receive it, and 97% are expected to get the full amount.

items.title: Less investor competition for first home buyers
items.body: Treasury forecasts the reforms will shift around 75,000 homes from investors to first home buyers over the next decade, with price growth moderating for a couple of years.

items.title: Revenue redirected to housing supply
items.body: The Budget includes a $2 billion Local Infrastructure Fund for the roads, water and power that unlock new housing — and negative gearing stays fully available for new builds and affordable-housing investments, pointing investment at supply.
